title: Naruto's New Anime Finally Resurfaces — Big Announcement Set for NYCC
summary: After more than three years of silence, the long-delayed Naruto anime project is finally showing signs of life. Back in August 2026, Viz Media and Shueisha announced that the franchise would have a panel at New York Comic Con 2026, featuring an announcement about a "new project." Fans immediately hoped it was about the new anime first announced in 2023. On Sept. 29, two official Naruto accounts on X confirmed exactly that — the NYCC announcement will be about the new anime. The panel, titled "Naruto: What's Next," will take place on Oct. 10 from 6 to 7 p.m. EDT. Fans in attendance or watching online will be "the first to witness the latest news of the New Naruto TV Anime Limited Series." The remake was originally announced as part of the series' 20th anniversary, in the form of four special episodes using modern animation techniques. A 10-minute trailer showed iconic scenes updated with a modern look. The episodes were supposed to air in September 2023, but a delay was announced that August to improve quality. Some fans speculated that after the trailer's positive reception, the franchise decided to approve a full remake. However, animation studio Pierrot has been busy with Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War, which concludes on Oct. 26. That may have put the Naruto remake on hold. Now, after more than three years, fans will finally know what to expect. Whether it's just four episodes or a full remake, the project will surely be a success. The search for Team 7 has begun.
why_it_matters: For a generation that watches everything on streaming, this shows how fan demand — measured in views, posts and convention tickets — can keep a franchise alive decades after it started. It also shows how much power a single animation studio's workload has over what millions of viewers eventually get to see.

background_read: Naruto is a Japanese manga — a comic read right to left — created by Masashi Kishimoto, about a young ninja who dreams of becoming his village's leader, the Hokage.

The series is published in Japan by Shueisha, the company behind the magazine Weekly Shonen Jump, and licensed in North America by Viz Media, which translates Japanese comics and animation for English-speaking fans.
The anime itself is made by Pierrot, a Japanese animation studio that also produces Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War — which explains why one show's schedule can stall another.
New York Comic Con (NYCC) is a huge annual fan convention in the United States, where publishers and studios rent stages called panels to reveal trailers and news to packed crowds.

Long waits are normal in anime: studios juggle several series at once, and a title can sit unfinished for years. In Naruto, 'Team 7' means the main trio of young ninjas — Naruto, Sasuke and Sakura — and their teacher Kakashi, so the article's final line is a wink to long-time fans.

perspectives.description: After three years of silence, the wait is finally paying off with a concrete date and stage. Modern animation could introduce iconic scenes to a whole new audience, and the trailer's warm reception suggests the project has real backing.

Three years with almost no updates feels like poor communication, and a single panel can end up being mostly marketing. If the panel reveals only four episodes rather than a full remake, many fans will feel the long wait was oversold.

Anniversary remakes and 'quality delays' are an established pattern in Japanese animation, where a small number of studios carry many hit series at once. The story is really about production capacity, not just hype.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what happens after the panel
perspectives.description: If the revival performs well, expect more remakes, spin-offs and merchandise from the franchise, and possibly the project being handed to a different studio or partner. Streaming and licensing deals will decide how quickly global fans actually get to watch it.
